# configuration tiers


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

### What this measures

litesearch offers many choices: four chunk sizes, five encoders, late
chunking, a document tree, an entity graph, clustering, a reranker, and
two ways to prepare a keyword query. This notebook reports which
combination works best for each of three kinds of document, and groups
the results into configuration tiers, from a keyword-only setup with no
model up to the most expensive one.

The measurements come from `python -m evals.run`, in
[`evals/`](https://github.com/Karthik777/litesearch/tree/main/evals). It
builds 45 stores and takes hours, so the harness lives there and this
notebook only prints its tables. The full report and the tier
definitions are in
[`docs/rag_tiers.md`](https://github.com/Karthik777/litesearch/blob/main/docs/rag_tiers.md).
The cells are `eval: false` and have no saved output; run them from the
repository root after the harness has run.

Several defaults have changed since this was measured, and partly
because of it.
[`chunk_markdown`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#chunk_markdown)
now cuts at 512 bytes, `db.search` now sends its keyword query through
[`pre()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pre), late
chunking was deleted (its code is in `evals/latechunk.py`), and the
graph leg was removed from `context`. Where the sections below describe
a default, they describe the one in place at the time.

The three genres were chosen because each breaks retrieval in a
different way:

The astro-ph papers are there on purpose. They talk about Mars,
conjunctions and ascending nodes, but not in the way the astrology books
do, so they test whether a retriever tells the genres apart or only
matches words.

### Ground truth without an LLM

Each query starts from a sentence that occurs exactly once in the
corpus, so the passage and the section it belongs to are known. The
sentence is then reworded in five flavours of increasing difficulty:
`verbatim`, `degraded`, `keyword`, `paraphrase` and `kw_para`. All five
are built from the same source sentences, so every comparison here is
paired: two configurations are always scored on the same questions.

A result is scored by word 5-grams, runs of five words, that occur in
only one section. That works at three levels (passage, section and
document), and it does not change when the chunk size does, which
matters because chunk size turns out to be the variable with the largest
effect. Most tables report section MRR: the mean over queries of 1
divided by the rank of the first result from the right section.

``` python
from evals import tables, report as R
from evals.queries import build as build_queries, FLAVOURS, overlap
print(tables._corpus())
```

``` python
qs = build_queries('astrology')
for fl in FLAVOURS: print(f'{fl:<11} {qs[3][fl]}')
```

### 1. Chunk size

The four settings are `page` (one chunk per page) and chunks of at most
1,024, 512 and 256 characters, cut by chonkie’s `RecursiveChunker`. This
was the largest effect in the whole evaluation. When it ran, the default
chunker was `FastChunker(chunk_size=4096)` and `add_doc` fed it one
section at a time, so on pages of 1,700 to 3,500 characters it almost
never split anything: the default behaved like `page`. The default is
now 512, counted in UTF-8 bytes: 512 characters of English, about 170 of
Devanagari.

``` python
print(R.summary('grain', ['genre','chunking','encoder','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))
```

### 2. Encoder

An encoder turns text into an embedding, a vector of numbers placed so
that texts with similar meaning sit close together. The five encoders
tested, `potion-32M`, `bge-small`, `jina-v2-sm`, `egemma-300m` and
`nomic-v1.5`, span three orders of magnitude of cost per chunk. All
produce float16 vectors and all ran on the same 4 CPU cores.

``` python
print(R.summary('encoder', ['genre','encoder','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))
```

### 3. Retrieval strategy

A strategy is how the keyword side and the vector side of a search are
run and combined. When this was measured, `db.search` quoted each token
of the query, which made its keyword query match only rows holding every
token. [`pre()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pre)
turns a query into keywords with wildcards joined by OR, and the caller
had to know to apply it. `db.search` now applies it by default
(`fts_pre=True`).

``` python
print(R.summary('strategy', ['genre','encoder','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))
```

### 4. Structure

A flat store, the document tree, and the tree rebuilt with headings
recovered from the PDF, since PDF conversion loses most of them.

``` python
print(R.summary('structure', ['genre','mode','encoder','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))
```

### 5. Late chunking

Late chunking embeds a whole document with a long-context encoder and
then splits the result into chunk vectors, so each chunk’s vector
carries some of its surroundings. It measured worse than embedding
chunks on their own and has since been deleted.

``` python
print(R.summary('late', ['genre','mode','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))
```

### 6. The graph leg

A third ranked list, built by walking a graph of the entities that
chunks mention, fused with the keyword and vector lists. It measured
negative and is no longer part of `context`; it lives on in
[vruksha](https://github.com/vedicreader/vruksha).

``` python
print(R.summary('graph', ['genre','strategy','graph_w'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))
print(R.summary('graph_notopic', ['genre','mode','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='same graph, topic nodes removed'))
```

### 7. Clustering

Clustering is judged here as a map of the corpus, by whether its groups
follow the genres and sections, not by whether it improves ranking.

``` python
print(tables._cluster())
```

### 8. One store or three

All three genres in one store against one store per genre. The second
table reports how many of the top 10 hits come from the wrong genre.

``` python
print(R.summary('mixed', ['genre','mode','encoder','strategy'], 'u_mrr', label='section MRR'))
print(R.summary('mixed', ['genre','mode','encoder','strategy'], 'cross_genre', label='share of top-10 hits from the wrong genre'))
```

Indexing time and query latency for each configuration.
